questions.q: How does this lesson distinguish deduplication from the broader matching concept in Lesson 6?
options: Deduplication is matching applied specifically within a single system or dataset, rather than across multiple systems
Deduplication and matching are completely unrelated processes
Deduplication only applies to reference data, never master data
Deduplication is a synonym for golden record creation
questions.explain: The lesson defines deduplication as the narrower case of matching, scoped to finding duplicates that already exist within one system or dataset.

questions.q: Which of these is listed as a common cause of duplicate records?
options: A customer signing up through a website form, then again through a call center agent who didn't find the existing record
A database being backed up nightly
A report being exported to PDF
A system being upgraded to a newer software version with no data changes
questions.explain: Multiple entry points creating separate records for the same person is explicitly listed as a common cause of duplicates, alongside migrations and missing real-time checks.

questions.q: What is the second step in the deduplication process described in this lesson?
options: Deleting all flagged records immediately with no review
Deciding which values survive for each duplicate group — the subject of survivorship rules
Running the blocking step from Lesson 6
Notifying every customer about the change
questions.explain: The three-step process is: find duplicate groups, decide which values survive (survivorship rules), then merge or link the records.

questions.q: What is the difference between 'cleanup' and 'prevention' in this lesson's deduplication discussion?
options: They are the same thing described with two different words
Cleanup is reactive, fixing existing duplicates periodically; prevention is proactive, checking for a near-match at the point of entry before a duplicate is created
Cleanup only applies to reference data; prevention only applies to master data
Prevention is always impossible to implement in practice
questions.explain: Cleanup addresses the existing backlog of duplicates reactively, while prevention stops new duplicates from forming by checking at the moment a record is created.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what determines whether duplicate records are physically merged or kept separate but linked by a shared ID?
options: Random selection with no governing factor
The MDM architecture style in use (e.g., registry style tends to link, consolidation/centralized styles tend to merge)
The day of the week the duplicates were found
Whether the records contain reference data
questions.explain: The lesson ties the merge-vs-link decision back to the architecture styles from Lesson 3 — registry style keeps source records in place and linked, while consolidation/centralized styles physically combine them.
